questions.q: State the formula for equivalent resistance when three resistors \(R_1, R_2, R_3\) are connected in series and when they are connected in parallel. Give the SI unit of equivalent resistance.
questions.a: Series: \(R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\); Parallel: \(\frac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3}\); Unit: ohm (Ω). A wrong answer (e.g., using product-over-sum for series or adding reciprocals for parallel) reveals confusion between the two combination rules and inability to recall the defining characteristic: same current in series, same voltage in parallel.

questions.q: Explain why the equivalent resistance of a parallel combination is always smaller than the smallest individual resistor, while the equivalent resistance of a series combination is always larger than the largest individual resistor.
questions.a: In parallel, multiple current paths are added, increasing total conductance (\(G = 1/R\)), so equivalent resistance decreases below the smallest branch resistance. In series, the current must pass through all resistors sequentially, adding their resistances, so equivalent resistance exceeds the largest individual resistance. A wrong answer (e.g., "parallel adds resistance") shows the student memorizes formulas without understanding the physical meaning of conductance and current division.

questions.q: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 6 Ω are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. Calculate (a) the equivalent resistance, (b) the total current drawn from the battery, and (c) the current through the 3 Ω resistor.
questions.a: (a) \(\frac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{6} = 1 \Rightarrow R_{\text{eq}} = 1\ \Omega\). (b) \(I_{\text{total}} = \frac{V}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{12\ \text{V}}{1\ \Omega} = 12\ \text{A}\). (c) \(I_{3\Omega} = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{12\ \text{V}}{3\ \Omega} = 4\ \text{A}\). A wrong answer (e.g., \(R_{\text{eq}} = 11\ \Omega\) by adding) indicates the student applied the series formula to a parallel circuit. A wrong current division (e.g., using \(I_{\text{total}} \times \frac{R_{\text{eq}}}{R}\)) shows misunderstanding of current divider rule.

questions.q: A circuit consists of a 4 Ω resistor in series with a parallel combination of 6 Ω and 3 Ω resistors. The combination is connected to a 24 V battery. Find the voltage across the 6 Ω resistor.
questions.a: Parallel equivalent: \(\frac{1}{R_p} = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow R_p = 2\ \Omega\). Total resistance: \(R_{\text{eq}} = 4 + 2 = 6\ \Omega\). Total current: \(I = \frac{24}{6} = 4\ \text{A}\). Voltage across parallel combination: \(V_p = I \times R_p = 4 \times 2 = 8\ \text{V}\). Since 6 Ω and 3 Ω are in parallel, voltage across 6 Ω = 8 V. A wrong answer (e.g., 24 V or 12 V) reveals the student cannot isolate the parallel sub-circuit or misapplies voltage division.

questions.q: A student claims: "In a series circuit with two resistors of different values, the larger resistor dissipates more power. In a parallel circuit with the same two resistors, the larger resistor also dissipates more power." Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is **false** for parallel. In series, same current \(I\) flows, so \(P = I^2R\) → larger \(R\) dissipates more power (true). In parallel, same voltage \(V\) applies, so \(P = V^2/R\) → larger \(R\) dissipates **less** power. A student who says "true for both" confuses the power formulas and fails to recognize that the conserved quantity changes from current (series) to voltage (parallel).

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a 9 V battery, three resistors (100 Ω, 220 Ω, 470 Ω), a multimeter, and connecting wires to verify the equivalent resistance formulas for series and parallel combinations. Describe the steps and the measurements you would take.
questions.a: Steps: (1) Measure each resistor individually with multimeter in ohmmeter mode (power off). (2) Connect them in series, measure total resistance between ends — should equal sum. (3) Connect them in parallel (all three leads joined at two common nodes), measure total resistance — should equal reciprocal of sum of reciprocals. (4) Optionally, connect battery, measure voltage across combination and total current with multimeter in ammeter mode, compute \(R = V/I\) and compare. A poor answer (e.g., "measure current only" or "connect battery while measuring resistance") shows lack of practical skill: ohmmeter requires no external voltage, and ammeter must be in series.
